name: Evergreen Protocol Definitions
description: Canonical definitions index for Evergreen Protocol v1.0 — the category standard for reference continuity governance.
usageNotice: Static versioned reference. Not a certification, compliance verdict, or live API endpoint.

terms.definition: The governance discipline of maintaining the validity, version integrity, citeability, and operational coherence of institutional reference systems — protocols, knowledge bases, evidence layers, and documentation — under accelerated change.
terms.boundaryNote: Reference continuity is the category Evergreen Protocol governs. It does not encompass information security, data governance, AI model safety, or content management.

terms.definition: The gradual loss of validity, citeability, or operational coherence in a reference system. Occurs silently through outdated content, undocumented changes, ambiguous ownership, or disconnection from the practices it governs. The primary risk that reference continuity governance addresses.

The challenge of maintaining reference validity in institutional environments where AI models, outputs, tools, team configurations, and regulatory frameworks change faster than the governance structures that depend on them. AI-era conditions accelerate reference decay; they do not constitute a separate governance category.

A versioned, citable reference that defines the scope, vocabulary, and explicit boundaries of a specific governance category. A category standard does not certify, audit, or impose legal obligations; it defines and documents a category.

A documented unit of governance with bounded scope, named roles, listed artifacts, acceptance criteria, and a defined review and versioning regime. A pattern for maintaining validity across time — not a claim about any specific technology or product category.
The structural layer: the formal elements — charter, roles, artifacts, acceptance criteria, change control — that give continuity a stable shape. Defines what may be built and audited.

The philosophical stance that unnecessary entropy — drift in definitions, tacit exceptions, ambiguous ownership, and decaying surfaces — is a manageable risk when made visible and reviewed. Justifies why explicit protocols must exist.
The operational commitment to tie reviews to validity and dependency change rather than fashion cycles or arbitrary urgency. Expressed concretely as review cadence and entropy checks.

The explicit statement of what a protocol governs and what it does not govern. Out-of-scope items should point to the responsible instrument: another protocol, contract, legal process, or technical standard.

Any object used as evidence of compliance or as an operational interface to the protocol: documents, registers, URLs, schemas, dashboards, logs, or system screens. If it cannot be located, it is not yet an artifact.
A testable condition that distinguishes compliant operation from non-compliance. Criteria must be observable and attributable to an owner.
The scheduled and event-triggered timetable for revisiting a protocol's truth: whether it still matches reality, whether artifacts align, and whether exceptions remain justified.
A structured examination during review for common drift modes: tacit exceptions, definition forks, surface drift, and ownership vacuums.
The accumulation of undocumented divergence between authoritative protocol text, operational practice, and external-facing surfaces or data definitions.

The role responsible for keeping protocol text coherent, scheduling reviews, and maintaining the change log. Maintainers propose changes; they do not unilaterally alter obligations without approver action unless explicitly delegated.
The role authorized to approve material changes and time-bounded exceptions. Approvers bear accountability for scope and risk tradeoffs.
The role accountable for artifact integrity: availability, accuracy, and traceability to the protocol version they support.
Any person or team obligated to operate under the protocol. Consumers are entitled to clarity, stable interfaces for change, and notice when obligations shift.
A documented, time-bounded deviation from a protocol requirement. Must state rationale, owner, expiry, and review trigger. Silent exceptions are defects, not informal flexibility.
A protocol update recorded with version number, date, author, summary, and accessible history. Semantic rules for major, minor, and patch are defined in the Methodology.
The degree to which operational reality matches the protocol's claims and artifacts. Validity is maintained by review, not by assertion.
A site or document set intended to be cited, audited, and reused across contexts. This property imposes obligations: stable URLs, explicit updates, and definitional discipline.

The structural readiness of an organization to demonstrate that its protocols, decisions, and knowledge assets were valid at the point of use. Strong evidence posture means an organization can answer: what was the governing reference, at what version, and who was responsible.

The practice of recording what changed in a reference system, when the change occurred, why it was made, and under whose authority — such that any prior state of the system can be identified and cited. The operational mechanism through which reference continuity is maintained.
